ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Norfolk, VA
ut.description: UT thickness surveys and ultrasonic weld inspection at Norfolk, VA shipyards, piers, plants and pressure equipment. Mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Norfolk, Virginia
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection (UT) for owners in Norfolk and the wider Hampton Roads area: steel on piers and cranes, ship and barge plating, pressure vessels, boilers, process piping and storage tanks. Technicians are mobilized to your site for a defined scope and report readings against the acceptance basis you name. Describe the asset, material and access through the UT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Norfolk

Norfolk is a harbor city on the Elizabeth River, and almost everything of industrial value here is steel exposed to salt air or salt water. Naval Station Norfolk occupies Sewells Point, private ship-repair yards work on the Elizabeth River, and the Virginia Port Authority runs Norfolk International Terminals nearby, with container cranes and rail-mounted gantries moving cargo across the quays. Add the coal export terminal at Lambert's Point and the barges and tugs that serve all of it, and the density of coated, wetted and splash-zone steel is unusual.

Ultrasonic thickness measurement is how owners keep track of what is left of that steel. Typical targets are hull and tank plating on commercial vessels in a repair period, ballast and fuel tank boundaries, pier and wharf steel, crane rail girders and boom sections, and the piping that runs through pump rooms and terminals. Inland from the water, hospitals, universities, food plants and manufacturers run boilers and pressure vessels that need periodic wall readings for insurance and jurisdictional inspection.

Ship and waterfront steel: what a Norfolk owner should know

Marine thickness work comes with a limit that is worth stating plainly. Atlantis holds no class-society approval for ship thickness measurement, so readings we take on a vessel support the owner's own decisions: pre-purchase checks, condition assessment between surveys, steel-renewal estimates before a drydock period and follow-up on a known wasted area. They are not submitted for credit to a class survey. If a surveyor needs class-credited gauging, the owner must engage a firm that the vessel's society has recognized for that task.

Naval work in the area follows the technical requirements written into each Navy contract. Those requirements, and who may perform the examination, are set by the contract and the shipyard, and this page does not claim to meet them. A commercial owner, a terminal operator, a marine contractor or a barge company can scope a UT survey with us directly.

What UT finds in Norfolk steel, and what it misses

A probe sends a pulse of sound through the wall, and the instrument measures the time for the echo from the opposite surface. Because sound speed in carbon steel is well known, that time converts to thickness. The method is excellent for general wall loss, localized pitting that is wide enough for the beam to sample, lamination in plate, and the remaining ligament under a wasted area. It works on any sound-conducting metal from one side only, so a tank can stay in service while its shell is surveyed.

The weak points are practical. Heavy scale, thick marine coatings and marine growth scatter or absorb sound, so the surface must be cleaned to a condition the procedure permits, or the instrument must be capable of measuring through a coating and verified on a sample. Very small pits can be missed by a single reading, which is why a grid is scanned rather than one point read. Rough or curved surfaces change coupling. Cast iron and coarse-grained castings attenuate the beam heavily. Cracks that lie parallel to the sound path are poor reflectors, and where surface-breaking cracks are the question another method fits better.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Hampton Roads work

Thickness work is governed by ASME Section V, where Article 23 carries the contact pulse-echo thickness practice SE-797, and by ASTM E797 for the same technique. Whether a measured wall is acceptable is not decided by the method: the answer comes from the minimum required thickness the owner or engineer has calculated, the corrosion allowance and the inspection plan for the equipment.

Weld examination follows Article 4 of Section V for the technique, with acceptance from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for pressure vessel welds, ASME B31.3 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 Clause 8 for structural groove welds. ASTM E164 covers contact UT of weldments. Where API 510, API 570 or API 653 applies, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record and Atlantis supplies the examination data, such as thickness at condition monitoring locations and indication sizes.

Virginia adds a jurisdictional layer. The Department of Labor and Industry runs the state boiler and pressure vessel safety program under Title 16, Agency 25, Chapter 50 of the Virginia Administrative Code. Boilers and pressure vessels must be ASME-built and registered with the National Board and the state, and routine inspections are carried out by insurance company inspectors, contract fee inspectors or owner-user inspectors holding Virginia commissions. A UT report can support that inspector's file, but it does not replace the jurisdictional inspection.

How a thickness survey is carried out

A survey begins with a plan: the component list, the measurement grid or condition monitoring locations, the materials, and the expected minimum. On site, the technician cleans each location, calibrates a dual-element probe on a step block of the same material as the part, and checks the calibration again at the end and whenever the probe or settings change. Dual-element probes suit corroded steel because the separate transmitter and receiver handle rough back walls better than a single element.

For hot lines on a ship's engine-room services or in a plant, high-temperature probes and couplant are used with a temperature correction, because sound moves more slowly in hot steel. Where the wall is thin or pitted, the technician watches the A-scan rather than trusting a digital number alone, since a doubled echo or a weak signal can show a false reading. Thicknesses are recorded against a grid or a labeled sketch so the next survey can repeat the exact same points, which is what turns individual readings into a corrosion rate.

Ultrasonic weld examination with angle beams

For weld volume, a wedge directs a shear wave into the material at a set angle, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees. The technician builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, scans the weld from both sides where access allows, and evaluates every indication against the reference. Lack of fusion, slag, cracks and incomplete penetration reflect sound in different ways, and the pattern of the echo as the probe moves is how the technician tells them apart.

Weld UT depends on geometry. Pipe branches, nozzle welds and thin walls need a technique worked out in advance, and the procedure should say how the weld cap is ground or how a dressed surface is handled. Where the construction code accepts UT in place of other volumetric methods, that substitution is agreed with the owner and engineer before work begins.

Who performs the work

Technicians who perform and interpret UT are qualified by Atlantis under its written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and evaluates results against the procedure. Procedures and report formats are approved by an ASNT Level III, and our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Each certification record stays with the employer, so qualification under SNT-TC-1A is a statement about the employer's program, not a portable license.

For work in Norfolk the usual preparation is a procedure written to the code you name, a review of drawings and materials before mobilization, and a confirmation of any badging, orientation or access rules at the yard, terminal or plant. If your own written practice already governs, our Level III consulting can review the procedure against it.

What the UT report contains

Every report names the component and its identification, the code and procedure with revision, the instrument and probe serial numbers, the calibration blocks and couplant used, the technician and certification level, the date and the surface condition. For thickness work it adds a grid or location sketch with each reading, the nominal and minimum required wall where you supply it, and flagged areas. For welds it lists each indication with position, length, amplitude against the reference and an accept or reject call against the named criteria.

Reports separate what was measured from what it means. Calculated corrosion rate and remaining life stay with the owner's engineer or authorized inspector, while the report gives them clean, repeatable data to work from.

Planning a UT job in Norfolk

Weather and water set the calendar. Summers are hot and humid, with a July average high around 87 degrees Fahrenheit and muggy air most days, which affects surface temperature on exposed steel and coating softness. Winters are windy and cold, with January lows averaging in the mid-30s, and cold steel changes couplant behavior. Verify the procedure's temperature range and plan couplant accordingly.

Access takes the longest to arrange. Piers, drydocks, terminal quays and crane structures need safety orientation, fall protection and sometimes escorts. Vessels in repair add hot work and confined-space entry. Tell us early whether the structure will be energized, whether scaffolding or lifts are provided and who will clean the surface, and travel for a mobilized crew can be arranged around those answers. Outage windows at area plants and ship repair periods are busy, so scope early.

UT, MT or PT for your Norfolk job

Choose UT when you need wall thickness, a corrosion survey, plate lamination or the inside of a weld. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Norfolk when the target is a surface or near-surface crack in carbon or low-alloy steel, such as a crane pin, a weld toe on a lifting lug or a hull attachment. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Norfolk for surface-breaking flaws on stainless steel, aluminum or other non-magnetic metals, which covers a lot of marine fittings.

Many jobs combine two: UT to size remaining wall at a wasted area, then MT or PT on a repair weld. The national ultrasonic testing service page lists general capabilities, and the ultrasonic testing guide explains the physics in more depth.

Training your own UT technicians

If your Norfolk operation wants a UT technician in house, start with UT Level 1 training and progress to UT Level 2 training. Atlantis supplies the training; your company issues the certification under its own written practice. The UT practical simulator gives trainees repeated scanning time before they touch real parts, and the Norfolk training page explains how theory, simulator work and hands-on practice at your facility fit together.

faq.q: What does UT inspection cost in Norfolk?
faq.a: The scope sets the fee, not a flat figure: component count, access, surface preparation, travel and the report format all matter. Send the details through the quote form and we respond with a scope-based quotation within one business day.

faq.q: Can Atlantis perform thickness measurements on ships in Norfolk?
faq.a: Yes, for owner decisions such as condition assessment, pre-purchase checks and steel-renewal estimates. Atlantis holds no class-society approval for ship thickness measurement, so those readings are not submitted for credit to a class survey.

faq.q: Does the work need a Level III on site?
faq.a: No. A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination under an approved procedure. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report format, and can be involved remotely or on site when the job calls for it.

faq.q: Which codes apply to ultrasonic weld inspection in Norfolk?
faq.a: The construction code for the item governs acceptance: ASME Section VIII Division 1 or B31.3 for pressure equipment and piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural steel. ASME Section V Article 4 supplies the examination technique.

faq.q: Can UT be done through paint or coating?
faq.a: Sometimes. Thin, well-bonded coatings may be measured through when the instrument and technique are verified on a sample of the same coating. Thick or blistered marine coatings usually need local removal first.

faq.q: How accurate is ultrasonic thickness measurement on corroded steel?
faq.a: Accuracy depends on calibration, surface condition and the probe. On clean, uniform steel readings are very repeatable. On pitted surfaces a single reading can miss the deepest pit, so grids and A-scan review are used to reduce that risk.

faq.q: Do you have an office in Norfolk?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city, and technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Scoping questions about access, badging and utilities are worked through before mobilization.

faq.q: Who decides whether a measured wall is acceptable?
faq.a: The owner, engineer or authorized inspector decides, using the minimum required thickness and applicable code. Atlantis reports measured data and flags readings below the value you provide, but does not set fitness for service.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do UT on a Navy vessel or at a naval facility?
faq.a: Naval contracts set their own technical and personnel requirements, and this service does not claim to satisfy them. Commercial vessels, contractors and waterfront owners in the region can request a scope directly.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Norfolk, VA | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MT) of welds, lifting gear and steel structures in Norfolk, VA yards, terminals and plants. Mobilized to site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Norfolk, Virginia
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MT, also called mag particle testing or MPI) for owners and contractors in Norfolk and Hampton Roads. Typical targets are welds on carbon and low-alloy steel, crane and rigging components, lifting lugs, pins and shafts, and repair welds at yards and terminals. Technicians travel to your site once the scope is set. Send the component list and procedure basis through the MT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Norfolk

Norfolk's economy is built around ships, piers and cargo handling, and that means a great deal of ferromagnetic steel carrying cyclic loads. Container terminals and the Virginia Port Authority's Norfolk International Terminals rely on cranes whose boom hinges, trolley frames and spreader connections see fatigue every working day. Ship repair yards along the Elizabeth River weld, grind and re-weld hull structure, foundations and attachments, and each repair weld may call for a surface examination before the vessel returns to service.

Away from the water, MT is part of routine work on pressure vessel nozzle welds, structural steel connections, heavy trailer and rail equipment, and the pins, hooks and shackles that make up lifting gear. Coal handling equipment at the Lambert's Point terminal and the conveyors, hoppers and structures that serve it are another field of steel where fatigue cracks start at weld toes and bolted joints.

What MT finds and what it misses

MT works by magnetizing the part. A crack or similar discontinuity that interrupts the magnetic field creates a leakage field at the surface, and fine iron particles gather there to form a visible indication. The method finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams and cold shuts, and can reveal discontinuities lying just under the surface. It is fast, shows the length and shape of an indication directly and works through thin non-magnetic coatings.

The limitation that decides every job is the material. MT only works on ferromagnetic steels, meaning carbon steel, low-alloy steel and most martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, bronze and nickel alloys cannot be magnetized well enough, so they need liquid penetrant testing in Norfolk instead; penetrant is the normal route for those metals. MT also misses flaws deeper than a short distance below the surface, and a crack lying parallel to the magnetic field gives almost no indication, which is why each area is examined with the field applied in two directions.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The technique comes from ASME Section V Article 7, and the details are explained in our Article 7 guide. ASTM E709 is the general guide and ASTM E1444 is the practice used on many contracts. Acceptance comes from the construction code: Appendix 6 of ASME Section VIII Division 1 for pressure vessels, paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 of ASME B31.3 for process piping, and the AWS D1.1 or D1.5 criteria for structural and bridge welding.

In Virginia, boilers and pressure vessels fall under the state Department of Labor and Industry program, with rules in Title 16, Agency 25, Chapter 50 of the Virginia Administrative Code. Equipment must be ASME-built and registered with the National Board, and inspections are performed by insurance company, contract fee or owner-user inspectors who hold Virginia commissions. Where API 510, 570 or 653 applies, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection, and Atlantis reports the examination data used in that file.

How the examination is performed

Preparation matters as much as magnetizing. Weld spatter, loose scale, heavy rust and grease are removed so particles can reach the surface and indications can form. Thick coatings may need local removal. For most field work the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke on the weld and the heat-affected zone, then repeats with the yoke turned about ninety degrees so cracks in any direction cross the field.

Yokes are checked before use against a lifting test: an alternating-current yoke must lift at least ten pounds at the pole spacing in use, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least forty pounds, per Article 7. Field strength is also confirmed with a pie-shaped or strip indicator. Dry visible powder suits warm, clean surfaces; wet particles, either visible or fluorescent, give better sensitivity on smooth parts. Fluorescent work needs a darkened area and a UV-A lamp whose intensity has been measured. After examination the part is demagnetized when a residual field would interfere with welding, machining or later operations, and the procedure states when that is needed.

Prods, yokes and wet particles: choosing a technique

A yoke is the default tool on ship and terminal steel because it leaves no arc strikes. Prods pass current through the part and can magnetize large castings or thick plate, but they can burn the surface and are restricted or banned on many specifications. Wet fluorescent MT is common in workshops on pins, shafts and small fabrications, where a portable UV lamp and a shaded corner of a shop floor are enough.

Underwater MT of piers or hulls is a specialist operation requiring divers and is not part of this service. Everything described here is carried out in air, on accessible steel, to the written procedure agreed beforehand.

Crane, rigging and lifting-gear examinations

Lifting equipment is the most frequent MT subject on a working waterfront. Hooks, shackles, padeyes, sling pins, sheave shafts and crane hinge pins are forged or machined carbon and alloy steel, they carry repeated heavy load, and their failure modes start as fine fatigue cracks at fillets, keyways and thread roots. MT shows those cracks long before they threaten the load path. A periodic examination program, with each part cleaned, magnetized and recorded against its identification, gives the owner a history of the part rather than a single pass-fail snapshot.

Disassembly is often the difficult part. A pin examined in place may have its critical zone hidden under a bushing, so the examination scope should state whether the pin is removed first. Atlantis can examine accessible faces on site, and the owner or crane maintenance contractor handles rigging, lockout and any component removal. The inspection criteria for the lifting equipment itself come from the equipment manufacturer, the owner's program or the governing crane standard, and the technician applies the limit stated in the contract.

Repair welds and grind-outs

Another common job is checking a repair. When a crack or defect is ground out of steel, MT confirms that the excavation has reached sound metal before welding begins, and again after the repair weld is complete and dressed. Doing the first check saves repeated weld cycles; doing the second documents the final condition. Because MT is quick, a technician can work alongside a welder and examine each stage without holding up the schedule.

On pressure-retaining steel, preheat and post-weld heat treatment affect what happens next. Particles do not tolerate high surface temperature, so the part must cool within the procedure's allowable range before wet or dry examination. Where a repair has been made to a boiler or pressure vessel, the National Board Inspection Code and the state jurisdiction control who may accept the repair, and our report is data for that decision.

Who performs the work

Atlantis technicians who carry out MT are qualified under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician selects the technique, performs the examination, interprets indications and records results. An ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and the report format. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer issues certification, and in this case that employer is Atlantis for its own staff.

Where your company has its own written practice or a customer-specified procedure, we can work to it after a review. The written practice development service helps owners who need a procedure built to a stated code.

What the MT report contains

Reports identify the component, location and drawing reference, the procedure and revision, the magnetizing equipment and its calibration status, the particle type and carrier, the field direction and number of passes, the technician and level, and the surface preparation and temperature. Each indication is described by location, length and orientation with a photograph or sketch, followed by an accept or reject call against the named criteria. Parts that required demagnetizing are noted.

For fatigue-critical items such as crane pins or lifting lugs, the report can record each examined face so a later inspection can compare the same locations.

Planning an MT job in Norfolk

Humidity is the main local factor. Summer air in Hampton Roads is muggy, with a typical July high near 87 degrees Fahrenheit, so wet surfaces, condensation on cooled steel and sweat-soaked gloves all change particle behavior and visibility. Winter brings windy conditions and January lows averaging in the mid-30s, so very cold steel needs the procedure's lower temperature limit confirmed before the wet method is used. Outdoor work at a pier or terminal is easier in the early part of the working day when sun glare is lower, particularly for visible particles.

Access and safety orientation at terminals, drydocks and plants should be arranged in advance, and electrical safety rules often govern the use of a mains-powered yoke near water. Give us the working surface, the power available and whether wet work is allowed, and travel is planned around those details.

MT, PT or UT for your Norfolk job

Use MT for crack-finding on ferromagnetic welds and parts. Use PT when the metal is stainless, aluminum or any non-magnetic alloy, or when the area is too awkward to magnetize. Use UT in Norfolk when thickness or subsurface weld quality is the question rather than a surface crack. The MT versus PT comparison sets out the trade-offs, and the national MT service page summarizes general capability.

Training your own MT technicians

If your team wants in-house MT capability, MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training cover the theory and technique. Your company certifies under its written practice; Atlantis delivers the instruction. The Norfolk training page describes how that blends with hands-on practice at your facility.

faq.q: What is magnetic particle inspection used for in Norfolk?
faq.a: It is used to find surface and slightly subsurface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel: ship repair welds, crane components, lifting lugs, pins, structural connections and pressure vessel nozzle welds at yards, terminals and plants.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Not effectively. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and most non-ferrous alloys cannot be magnetized well enough for particles to gather, so those alloys are routed to dye penetrant inspection.

faq.q: Do you inspect underwater steel in Norfolk?
faq.a: No. Atlantis performs MT in air on accessible steel. Underwater examination needs diver support and is a separate specialist scope that is not offered through this service.

faq.q: How much surface preparation is required before MT?
faq.a: Loose scale, spatter, oil and heavy rust must come off so particles reach the metal. Thin tight coatings are often acceptable if the procedure allows it, while thick or flaking coatings need local removal.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: Yes, when a residual field would interfere with welding, machining, bearings or later service. The procedure states whether it is required, and the report records that demagnetizing was carried out.

faq.q: Which code sets the acceptance criteria for MT in Norfolk?
faq.a: The construction code or contract governs, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. ASME Section V Article 7 supplies the technique, not the pass-fail limit.

faq.q: Can you work to a Navy or customer-specific MT procedure?
faq.a: We can review a customer procedure and work to it when our written practice and personnel meet its stated requirements. Naval contracts have their own rules, which this service does not claim to satisfy.

faq.q: How do I request an MT quote for a Norfolk job?
faq.a: Send component details, material, code basis, access and timing through the quote form. We reply within one business day with questions or a scope-based quotation, and technicians travel to your site.

faq.q: Does Atlantis staff an office in Norfolk?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians are mobilized to your site, and access, safety orientation and power supply are confirmed with you before they travel.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Norfolk, VA | LPT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing (PT) of welds and machined parts in stainless, aluminum and steel at Norfolk, VA yards and plants. Mobilized to site. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Norfolk, Virginia
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection or PT, for owners and contractors in Norfolk and across Hampton Roads. Penetrant testing finds flaws that are open to the surface on welds, castings, forgings and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel alike. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the defined scope. Send the component list and acceptance basis through the PT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Norfolk

Hampton Roads has a long maritime repair tradition, and the metals involved are rarely all magnetic. Vessels in a repair period carry stainless piping, aluminum superstructure and fittings, bronze and nickel-copper valve bodies, propulsion components and heat exchanger shells. Where a weld has been repaired on any of these, PT is the straightforward way to confirm that no crack remains open at the surface. Shipyards along the Elizabeth River, barge and tug operators, and marine contractors all have that need.

Farther from the water, penetrant work goes into food and beverage plants with stainless process lines, hospital and university boiler rooms, chemical and fuel handling facilities, and fabrication shops building tanks, skids and frames. Terminal equipment such as stainless hydraulic fittings, small castings on cranes and machined pins also come through for periodic checks. PT suits all of them because it does not depend on the alloy being magnetic.

What PT finds and what it misses

A low-viscosity liquid is drawn into any crack, pit or lap that reaches the surface. After excess penetrant is removed, a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out, producing a visible mark much wider than the flaw itself. This makes PT sensitive to tight cracks that are hard to see by eye, including fatigue cracks, shrinkage cracks, grinding cracks and weld toe cracking.

The limitation is built into the physics. Only surface-breaking discontinuities can be found, so a crack buried below the surface or sealed by smeared metal produces nothing. Porous materials such as some castings, sintered parts and rough or oxidized surfaces trap penetrant and create background that hides indications. Shot-blasted or heavily ground surfaces can smear metal over the opening of a crack, so the preparation method is part of the procedure. Wall thickness and internal weld quality are outside what PT can say, and UT in Norfolk covers those.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The technique is set out in ASME Section V Article 6, which our Article 6 guide explains, and ASTM E165 is the practice widely cited for general industry. Pressure vessel work uses Appendix 8 of ASME Section VIII Division 1, process piping uses paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 of ASME B31.3, and structural steel is judged against AWS D1.1 where it specifies PT.

Virginia regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Department of Labor and Industry under Title 16, Agency 25, Chapter 50 of the Virginia Administrative Code. Equipment must be built to ASME rules and registered with the National Board and the state. Inspections are carried out by insurance company inspectors, contract fee inspectors and owner-user inspectors with Virginia commissions, and the Department issues the certificate after a satisfactory report. A PT report is supporting data for that file, and Atlantis does not act as the jurisdictional inspector.

How a penetrant examination is carried out

The sequence is fixed and every step has a minimum dwell. First comes cleaning: solvent, detergent or mechanical methods strip oil, paint, scale and weld residue, and the part dries completely, because trapped water or solvent blocks penetrant entry. Next, penetrant is applied and left for the dwell time in the procedure, long enough for the liquid to enter tight cracks. Excess is then removed, either by solvent wipe on field jobs or by water rinse where the process allows, taking care not to wash penetrant out of the defects themselves.

Developer is applied in a thin even layer, and the technician examines the surface after the development time. Visible-dye systems with a red penetrant and white developer are the standard in the field. Fluorescent penetrant gives more sensitivity but needs a darkened space and a UV-A lamp, so it is usually kept for shop work. After examination the surface is cleaned again to remove residue that could cause corrosion or contaminate later welds, an important point for stainless piping and for low-chloride requirements.

Temperature, surface and material limits

Article 6 sets a standard window of roughly forty to one hundred twenty-five degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside it the procedure must be qualified at the temperature in use, normally by comparing results on a reference block. That matters here more than people expect: a steel hull plate in a Hampton Roads July can pass that window by midday, and a winter morning on an open pier can fall below it, so surface temperature is measured and recorded rather than guessed.

Material compatibility is another consideration. On stainless steel and nickel alloys, penetrant materials are often required to be low in halogens and sulfur, with lot certifications on file. On aluminum and titanium, similar controls apply. The procedure names the product family so there are no surprises when the report is reviewed.

Marine fittings, valve bodies and small castings

Penetrant testing is often the practical choice for the small, awkward parts that fill a vessel or terminal. Valve bodies, strainers, pump casings, bronze and nickel-copper fittings, rudder and propulsion hardware, and aluminum brackets are difficult or impossible to magnetize, yet a crack in any of them can cause a leak or a failure under load. PT handles irregular shapes because the liquid flows into any opening, regardless of geometry or orientation, and the developer shows the result without special equipment.

Castings need a word of caution. Many marine castings are porous at the surface, and penetrant can bleed from shrinkage porosity and look like a defect. A technician experienced with castings knows which indications are expected in the casting specification and which are cracks, and the report distinguishes relevant from non-relevant findings. Where the acceptance standard for a casting allows a certain amount of porosity, the report records what was seen and how it was judged.

Stainless piping, tank repairs and weld cleanliness

Food, chemical and fuel facilities around Norfolk run stainless piping and tanks, where cleanliness is as important as crack detection. After a repair weld or modification, PT is used on the finished root or cap surface, and residual penetrant must be fully removed so it cannot contaminate product or promote corrosion later. The procedure states the cleaning agent, the rinse, the drying step and whether a final verification is needed, and the report records that the post-examination cleaning was done.

Fit-up inspection and weld-prep checks use the same principle: penetrant on a bevel face can show laminations or cracks before welding begins. For storage tanks, PT is commonly applied to repair welds on shells and nozzles after grinding, as part of the repair package the owner's authorized inspector accepts. The owner decides the acceptance basis and who signs off, while we supply the data and the technician's findings.

Who performs the work

PT technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician carries out the sequence, interprets indications and records them, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and the report format. Qualification under that practice belongs to the employer; it is not a license that follows a person to another company.

When a customer has its own procedure or a code-specified one, we review it first. For owners who still need a procedure written, the Level III consulting service and the written practice service are available.

What the PT report contains

A report identifies the item and location, the drawing or weld number, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system and lot numbers, the cleaning method, the surface and part temperature, the dwell and developing times and the technician and level. Indications are described with location, shape and size and photographed with a scale where possible. The final call, accept or reject, is made against the criteria named in the contract, with relevant indications distinguished from non-relevant ones such as machined edges or rust streaks.

Planning a PT job in Norfolk

Weather needs more planning for PT than for most methods. Summer humidity and heat can cause solvents to flash off before dwell is complete, while winter cold slows penetrant and developer behavior and condensation forms on cold steel as warmer air moves in. Wind blows dust and salt spray onto prepared surfaces, so open work is often screened or timed. In the yard or on a pier, prepared surfaces should be examined soon after cleaning, because a salt film can form within hours and interfere with the result.

Access and housekeeping are also practical points. Terminals, drydocks and plants usually require orientation, and some areas restrict solvents and open containers. Tell us about ventilation, hot work nearby and waste handling, and technicians will be mobilized with the right materials. If the surface needs grinding or blasting first, say who will do it and how, since the preparation method affects whether cracks stay open.

PT, MT or UT for your Norfolk job

Choose PT for non-magnetic metals, small complex shapes and any surface where cracks are the concern. Choose MT in Norfolk for carbon and low-alloy steel when you want faster, more sensitive crack detection and slightly subsurface capability. Choose UT for thickness or internal weld quality. The MT versus PT comparison goes through the decision, and the national PT page gives an overview of the service.

Training your own PT technicians

For in-house capability, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training cover the theory and technique, and the PT practical simulator lets trainees practice the sequence before handling real parts. Your company certifies its own staff under its written practice. See the Norfolk training page for how the pieces fit together.

faq.q: What is dye penetrant inspection used for in Norfolk?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks and porosity on welds, castings and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel, which suits ship repair, marine fittings, food plants, boiler rooms and fabrication shops.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: No. Liquid is drawn only into flaws that break the surface. Subsurface cracks, internal lack of fusion and wall loss need other methods such as ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Does the metal have to be magnetic for PT?
faq.a: No, that is its advantage. PT works on non-porous materials whether they are magnetic or not, so it covers stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, bronze and nickel alloys that MT cannot examine.

faq.q: Can PT be done outdoors in Norfolk weather?
faq.a: Yes, within the procedure's temperature range and with wind, rain and salt spray controlled. Surface and part temperature are measured and recorded, and work is paused or shielded if conditions fall outside what the procedure allows.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much for PT?
faq.a: Oil, paint, scale and smeared metal can block a crack opening, which hides a real flaw. Grinding or blasting can also close defects, so the preparation method is written into the procedure.

faq.q: Do you use special penetrant materials on stainless steel?
faq.a: Where the specification requires it, yes. Stainless and nickel alloy work often calls for low-halogen, low-sulfur products with lot certification, which are named in the procedure and the report.

faq.q: Which code gives acceptance limits for PT?
faq.a: The construction code or contract does, for example ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. ASME Section V Article 6 describes the method but does not set pass-fail limits.
